lesson_title: Every Karoo Koppie Is a Factory With a Rubble Chute
hook_text: Hills in South Africa don't wear down. They walk backwards. Here's the machine that moves them.
clip_script: Next long drive, look at any Karoo koppie and you will see the same four-part machine, top to bottom, every single time. At the top, a rounded scalp — the crest, slowly balding as weathering loosens its grains. Below it, a face of bare rock — the cliff, and it is the hill's factory: this is where solid rock gets broken off and dropped. Geographers call it the free face because whatever breaks loose falls immediately — nothing stays behind to soften it. Under the factory hangs the rubble chute — the talus. Every block the cliff drops lands here, and the pile sets itself at the steepest angle loose stone can hold, about 25 to 35 degrees — the exact same angle a heap of builder's sand chooses, no matter how you pour it. Tip on more rubble and it slides until the resting angle returns, which is why the chute is perfectly straight. And at the bottom, a long gentle apron of rock sweeping out to the plain — the pediment. Now the twist: this machine makes the hill WALK. The factory face sheds rock and steps backward. The chute follows. The apron grows into the space they left. And the profile never slumps — cliff stays sheer, chute stays straight, apron stays gentle. Run it for fifty million years and the aprons of walking hills meet to form the great Karoo flats, with every last koppie still marching. Scalp, factory, chute, apron. Four parts, one walking machine.
visual_style: A clean cross-section of a koppie building itself element by element with the four labels stamping on, then the whole profile sliding backwards in time-lapse as the pediment stretches, ending on a real Karoo horizon with ghost outlines of where the hills used to stand.
mood: Mechanical satisfaction — a landscape revealed as a working machine.
pacing: Four crisp beats for the four elements, then a slow widening pull as deep time runs.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and label any hillside in the country on sight.
